name: Erigeron

project_scope.source_pool_synonym: Conyza canadensis maps to Erigeron canadensis, no duplicate species card
project_scope.science_status: Preserve previously published UNRESOLVED range statuses of geiseri and modestus; horseweed independently pending 3-county verification
project_scope.lesson_scope: Three species confirmed installed in current canonical manifest; E. philadelphicus and E. strigosus are source-pool candidates only, not installed. Native-range evidence remains unchanged.

look_here_first: LOOK HERE FIRST: 1) inspect full rooted plant (horseweed annual/winter-annual rosette → tall leafy stem); 2) check NARROW ALTERNATE stem leaves and strongly terminal branching; 3) with hand lens, distinguish fresh tiny heads with involucres about 3–4 mm LONG and rays ~0.5–1 mm from larger showy-rayed fleabanes; 4) recognize the white pappus as LATER FRUIT, not flowers. E. geiseri is annual with slender taproot; E. modestus has woody perennial base.
shared_traits: Asteraceae composite capitula with many minute florets
Alternate leaves on horseweed (other Erigeron leaf architecture varies)
Wind dispersed one-seeded cypsela with white pappus hairs
Flowering head size and ray length more discriminating than common name

comparison_matrix.horseweed: Annual or winter annual; often one erect main stalk 50–200 cm, branches mainly at TOP
comparison_matrix.fleabanes: Many Erigeron spp. have smaller branched stems arising from basal rosette, but can overlap
comparison_matrix.photo_need: Full rooted plant with lower stem and flowering arrangement

comparison_matrix.horseweed: Numerous tiny heads with INVOLUCRES about 3–4 mm LONG; short pale rays ~0.5–1 mm can be inconspicuous. Avoid treating mature white seed fluff as fresh rays.
comparison_matrix.fleabanes: Often larger daisy-like heads with visibly extending white or lavender rays
comparison_matrix.photo_need: Fresh OPEN flowering head front + side, millimeter ruler; a fruit pappus picture does not prove ray length.

comparison_matrix.horseweed: Narrow sessile linear-oblanceolate stem leaves, frequently shallowly toothed low down
comparison_matrix.fleabanes: Often broader basal leaves, fewer cauline leaves in some species
comparison_matrix.photo_need: Leaf at lower, middle, upper nodes with scale

comparison_matrix.horseweed: Many tiny cypselae with white pappus 2–3 mm
comparison_matrix.fleabanes: Also pappus fruit — not independently diagnostic
comparison_matrix.photo_need: Single head and seed after flowering

lookalike_warnings: Conyza canadensis is an older/alternative genus combination, not a second horseweed species.
Conyza bonariensis and C. sumatrensis may appear as lookalikes in disturbed plants, but detailed head/hair characters needed; don't claim all are local or native.
Erigeron geiseri and Erigeron modestus already have separate species cards; only add horseweed as one new taxon.
Horseweed tiny flowers are not goldenrod: goldenrod has YELLOW composite heads with much more showy yellow rays.

part_examples.title: 1 · Begin with the winter rosette
part_examples.look_for: The larger notched/toothed-leaved rosette is horseweed. A SMALL separate Draba verna rosette is also in the frame; do not label both species as horseweed.
part_examples.why_it_matters: A rosette-only ID should remain provisional; return to the same plant when it bolts.

part_examples.title: 2 · Trace the upright leafy stem
part_examples.look_for: Follow the tall single stem, alternate narrow leaves and many upward branches ending in tiny pale heads.
part_examples.why_it_matters: Shows horseweed's mature architecture and how it differs from daisy-like fleabanes.

part_examples.title: 3 · Fruiting pappus macro (NOT open ray florets)
part_examples.role: Fruiting head: pappus and spent receptacle
part_examples.look_for: At center, a spent head; surrounding fine white filaments are PAPPUS attached to fruits. This specific photo does not show the short pale rays of an actively blooming horseweed head.
part_examples.why_it_matters: Pappus bristles are not petals; use a fresh flowering photo for ray-floret teaching.

part_examples.title: 4 · Find the feathery pappus
part_examples.look_for: Later wispy fruiting structure with pappus; broad green foreground blade is not confidently attributable to the photographed horseweed.
part_examples.why_it_matters: Connects flowers to dispersal and highlights a shared composite fruit character.

part_examples.title: 5 · NEED PHOTO — actual horseweed OPEN flowers vs showy fleabane
part_examples.look_for: Bring same-scale photos with a ruler: horseweed with green involucre ~3–4 mm LONG and very short fresh whitish marginal rays, versus E. strigosus or E. philadelphicus with obviously longer daisy-like rays.
part_examples.why_it_matters: A direct visual pair teaches how ray length and head architecture separate common confusions without mistaking flower color for a full ID.

genus_diagnostics.flower_heads: All Erigeron members are composite-family plants bearing capitula (flower heads with many little florets), not single big flowers. HORSEWEED has extremely small heads with barely visible short rays; many other fleabanes have obvious longer daisy-like rays. Don't generalize horseweed's almost rayless look to the whole genus.
genus_diagnostics.leaves: Often alternate simple foliage, but leaf shape varies greatly among fleabanes. Horseweed forms a rosette first, then alternate narrow stem leaves. Study BOTH seasons before identifying the species.
genus_diagnostics.stem: In horseweed a single upright, leafy main stem branches into a broad narrow-headed terminal panicle. Other Erigeron may be much shorter or hold one/several showier heads. Whole-plant architecture is important but not definitive alone.
genus_diagnostics.inflorescence: Compare head size, number, rays and the panicle shape. Horseweed has scores to hundreds of heads just a few millimeters across; many fleabanes have larger radiate heads that resemble tiny daisies.
genus_diagnostics.fruit: Mature Erigeron cypselae generally have a pappus aiding wind dispersal. The horseweed photograph shows fluffy mature heads; a single dry cypsela and attachment of bristles needs a millimeter-scale macro.
